title: Be strong in the Lord
meditation: Paul reminds us that our struggle is not only against people, but against the spiritual forces that try to weaken our faith and our calling.
The armor he describes is not for attacking others. It is truth, righteousness, readiness to proclaim the gospel of peace, faith, salvation and the word of God, all of which help us stand firm.
In the Gospel, Herod wants Jesus dead, yet Jesus does not panic. He keeps healing and teaching today and tomorrow, because he knows his mission will be completed in God's time.
Then he speaks with tenderness over Jerusalem, longing to gather its children as a hen gathers her brood, even though the city was not willing.
For us seminarians, the God who gives us armor also gives us shelter. When discouragement or temptation comes, we return to prayer and the Eucharist instead of trying to fight alone.
Paul asked the Ephesians to pray for him so that he could speak with boldness. Today let us pray for one another, for our teachers, and for the families who support our vocations.
Lord Jesus, clothe me in your truth and your peace today, and when I feel I must stand alone, gather me back under your care. Amen.

title: Love that grows with insight
meditation: Paul begins his letter to the Philippians by thanking God every time he remembers them, and he prays for them with joy.
He asks that their love may overflow more and more, growing in knowledge and full insight, so that they can judge what is best.
For Paul, love is not only a warm feeling. It must be guided by truth and sound judgment, so that we can choose what truly matters.
In the Gospel, Jesus goes to a meal at the house of a leading Pharisee on the Sabbath, and a man who is seriously ill stands before him.
Jesus asks the experts in the law whether it is lawful to heal on the Sabbath. They have no answer, so he heals the man and sends him home.
The Sabbath was given for the good of people, and Jesus shows that rules must serve love. Do I ever hold on to my rules at the cost of someone who needs help?
Lord, make my love grow in wisdom and sound judgment, so that I may serve others generously and choose what is good in your sight. Amen.

title: Be holy, for I am holy (1 Peter 1:15-16)
meditation: Dear brothers and sisters in Christ,

As we celebrate the Solemnity of All Saints today, allow me to begin this meditation with these words of exhortation from the Apostle Peter, who reminds us that holiness is the ultimate goal of the entire Christian life.

The saints whom we commemorate today were men and women of their own time. Like us, they experienced the joys and trials of human existence; like us, they believed in God and walked in faith. However, they left us a precious testimony through their lives, which remains a light and an encouragement on our journey towards God.

They form that vast and countless multitude presented to us in today's first reading. They now enjoy the fullness of happiness because they live in God's presence and are filled with His blessings. Indeed, the supreme joy of the saints consists in the beatific vision of God, in that eternal contemplation of the One who is the source of all love and happiness. Conversely, the greatest suffering of the damned consists precisely in being deprived forever of God's presence.

But we, dear brothers and sisters, are filled with firm hope: the hope that one day we shall behold the face of God and share in eternal happiness with all the saints who have gone before us. Saint John reminds us of this in the second reading: we are already children of God, although what we shall become has not yet been fully revealed. Nevertheless, we know that when Christ appears, we shall be like Him, because we shall see Him as He really is.

In the light of this hope, and in response to the invitation of the eight Beatitudes proclaimed in today's Gospel, let us strive, dear brothers and sisters, to make the Gospel the true light of our lives. Holiness is not an ideal reserved for a few extraordinary people; it is a vocation addressed to each and every one of us. It is built day by day through our choices, our words, our attitudes and, above all, through the way we love God and our neighbour.

May our actions, therefore, reflect the charity of Christ, so that at the end of our earthly pilgrimage, the Lord may address these words of promise to us: “Come, you who are blessed by my Father; inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world. For I was hungry and you gave me food; I was thirsty and you gave me drink; I was naked and you clothed me…” (Matthew 25:34–36).

May our patron saints intercede for us, accompany us through their prayers, and obtain for us the grace to follow Christ faithfully, until the day when we shall be united with them in the glory of the Kingdom of Heaven.
A blessed and holy Feast of All Saints to everyone!

title: Commemoration of all departed souls
meditation: Today we celebrate the commemoration of all departed souls. It is with great hope that we join all believers in offering prayers for our beloved who have passed away.
This celebration is not new in the Catholic Church. It is drawn from the Jewish tradition of mourning, and in Christian antiquity people already prayed in the graveyards.
Saint Augustine encouraged Christians to pray for the departed on the day of their death or on chosen days (Sermon 172).

Saint Odilo instituted this day, 2 November, in the monastery of Cluny. It was later approved for the universal Church by Pope Leo IX in the 11th century, and became official in the universal Church in the 13th century.
Praying for the departed is a sign of faith in the afterlife, of love for those who have died, and of hope that we will join them in heaven.
The readings of today tell us that these earthly sufferings will have an end. This is what Job experienced: the assurance that the Savior is alive and will rescue him in all his distress.
Beloved, God is not indifferent to our human sufferings, including death. He hears our cries and answers us. Dying is a terrifying experience, but God is always near.
Jesus told his disciples not to be troubled, because in his Father's house there are many dwelling places, and whatever is asked in his name will be given to us.

My beloved in Christ, you are not alone in these difficult moments. May Jesus comfort you, and may we meet again our parents, brothers and sisters who have gone before us. We are pilgrims on earth, but we have an Advocate, and we are moved by faith.
Keep resting in peace! God grant eternal life to our departed friends, both those we know and those who are unknown to us.

title: Tuesday of the Thirty-First Week in Ordinary Time
meditation: Today, the Word of God invites us to remain ever open and ready to respond to God's call.

In our daily lives, it is all too easy to become caught up in numerous activities, some of which may seem indispensable, yet gradually lead us to overlook what is most essential: our life with God. This is often reflected in our relationship with Him, where our attachment to material possessions, money, and even family ties can sometimes become obstacles to our spiritual growth and Christian journey.

The twofold invitation in today's Gospel refers first to God's call to Israel and then to His invitation extended to all the nations. The Acts of the Apostles recounts this transition from Israel to the Gentiles, a decisive moment in the history of the Church, reminding us that God's salvation is intended for all humanity, without exception.

Dear brothers and sisters, the Lord invites us to walk with Him. He comes to meet us in great humility, as the first reading reminds us, so that He may become one of us and share in our human condition.
Let us therefore give Him our response and avoid every form of refusal. Indeed, the reasons that lead us to postpone or turn down God's invitations are not always beneficial to our lives.
May we never allow our earthly concerns to prevent us from welcoming the Lord into our hearts.
Wishing you all a blessed day!
Father Dieudonné MANIRAGUHA
